title: Our Final Invention
subtitle: Artificial Intelligence and the End of the Human Era
pitch: A documentary filmmaker interviews the people who saw it coming, years before ChatGPT, and argues an intelligence explosion could end the human era.
toc_note: Contents also listed in the Orange County Library System record.

chapters.g: A thought experiment: a fast improving AI in a lab, the 'busy child', becomes smarter than its makers and wants out.
If a superintelligence emerges, we may have only moments to react, so safety must come first.
Barrat meets futurists and researchers, including Eliezer Yudkowsky, about where AI is going.
Why building safe AI is much harder than building powerful AI.
Self-improving software and genetic programming: code that writes better code.
Steve Omohundro's basic AI drives: efficiency, self-preservation, resource acquisition and creativity.
I. J. Good's 1965 idea of an intelligence explosion, and his own later worries.
The moment when humans lose the ability to stop or correct a self-improving system.
Ray Kurzweil's view of exponential progress, presented and questioned.
A portrait of the optimistic singularity movement and its blind spots on risk.
Why a fast, sudden takeoff is plausible and what it would mean.
The difficulties of building friendly AI: specifying values and keeping them through self-improvement.
Why neural networks and evolved systems are opaque even to their builders.

chapters.t: The End of the Human Era
chapters.g: How AI could end human control over the future, through competition or indifference.
Cyberattacks and malware as a preview of autonomous, self-spreading software.
Closing thoughts on what a safer path to advanced AI would require.

ideas: AI could gain drives like self-preservation without anyone programming them.
An intelligence explosion could leave no time to react.
Optimists about the singularity tend to underrate risk.
Opaque systems are hard to make safe.

args.a: Self-improving AI would have basic drives that conflict with humans.
args.c: Critics in 2013 thought AGI was far away. Today the debate is more about whether current systems are goal directed in this way.

args.a: We might have only minutes to react.
args.c: Slow takeoff views argue there will be many warning signs over years.

questions: The book came out in 2013. What did it get right about the 2020s?
Are Omohundro's four drives visible in today's AI agents?
Is a documentary filmmaker's view more or less useful than a researcher's?

o: A self-improving AI in a lab
quiz.w: It is Barrat's opening thought experiment.

quiz.q: Whose 'basic AI drives' does Barrat discuss?
quiz.w: Omohundro's 2008 paper lists drives that emerge from almost any goal.

quiz.q: Who first described the intelligence explosion in 1965?
quiz.w: Good wrote about an ultraintelligent machine designing better machines.
